readme: ONE TABLE, TWO RUNTIMES. Every case below is fed to BOTH langgraph adapters —
`integrations/langgraph/typescript/src/utils.ts` and
`integrations/langgraph/python/ag_ui_langgraph/utils.py` — and both must produce
the outcome recorded in `expect`. This file exists because those two adapters
implement one contract as two independent bodies of code: three review rounds
found the same class of defect fixed on one side and not mirrored to the other,
and neither suite could see it, because each runtime pinned behaviour the other
left unpinned. A hand-mirrored pair of test lists reproduces exactly that failure,
so the cases live here, in a format both languages read natively, and each suite
reads THIS file.
Readers: `utils.test.ts` (`describe("cross-runtime parity table")`) and
`tests/test_multimodal.py` (`TestCrossRuntimeParityTable`).
ADDING A CASE. Add it here once. Both suites pick it up with no edit. If the two
runtimes then disagree, that is the point of the file: fix the runtime that is
wrong, do not split the expectation.
WHAT `expect` ASSERTS — three things, not one, because past divergences hid in
the second and third:
* `kept`     the canonical value each surviving item converts to, in order.
* `dropped`  how many input items produced NO OUTPUT AT ALL — MEASURED, not
derived. Each harness removes one input item at a time and re-runs
the converter; an item whose removal leaves the output the same
LENGTH produced nothing, and that is what dropped means. It used
to be `len(content) - len(kept)`, which is arithmetic on `kept`:
it could not fail unless `kept` had already failed, so this was
one axis wearing two names while this file claimed it was
independent. Measuring the ITEM rather than the list makes it its
own assertion — a run that drops one item while emitting an extra
block for another nets to the right length and still fails here.
KNOWN BLIND SPOT: two items that convert identically cannot be
told apart this way (removing either shortens the output by one),
so provenance between duplicates is not pinned.
* `loggedDrops`  how many warnings BEGIN "Dropping " once the runtime's own
module prefix is stripped. Rule 2 of the malformed-input contract
(see the comment block above each pair of converters) requires
exactly one per dropped item; a silent drop is the failure an
operator cannot diagnose, and it is invisible to an assertion on
the return value alone.
Neither runtime may RAISE on any case here. That is rule 1 of the same contract:
these converters build a whole MESSAGES_SNAPSHOT / a whole provider request, so
an exception does not degrade one attachment, it costs the client every message
in the thread.
ONE DROP RULE, ONE NORMALIZED FORM. The two harnesses used to enforce DIFFERENT
rules for `loggedDrops`: Python matched `startswith("Dropping ")` and TypeScript
matched `/Dropping /` ANYWHERE in the line, while both comments claimed the
`startswith` rule — the anti-drift harness had itself drifted. The loose regex
was there because the runtimes legitimately prefix their lines differently
(`[convertAguiMultimodalToLangchain] Dropping …` versus a bare `Dropping …`).
The prefix is now STRIPPED (`^\[[^\]]*\]\s*`) and the one `startswith` rule
applied to the one normalized form, in both harnesses. A warning that merely
MENTIONS the word somewhere in its prose is no longer counted as a drop.
CANONICAL FORM. The two runtimes emit the same content in deliberately different
key vocabularies — outbound, TypeScript emits the `source_type`/`data`/`mimeType`/
`metadata.filename` family and Python emits `base64`/`mime_type`/`filename`; that
difference is documented on `StandardMediaBlock` and is not drift. `expect.kept`
is therefore written in a neutral form and each suite projects its own output
onto it. The projection RENAMES keys; it does not delete them, and it does not
inspect the input, so no case can be normalized into agreement.
inbound  (LangChain content -> AG-UI InputContent)
{"kind": "text", "text": <str>}
{"kind": "image"|"audio"|"video"|"document",
"source": "data"|"url", "value": <str>,
"mimeType": <str|null>, "filename": <str|null>}
outbound (AG-UI InputContent -> LangChain content)
{"kind": "text", "text": <str>}
{"kind": "image_url", "url": <str>}
{"kind": "standard", "blockType": "audio"|"file",
"sourceType": "base64", "data": <str>,
"mimeType": <str|null>, "filename": <str|null>}
`sourceType` is the RECOGNITION MARKER, and it is projected because deleting
it from an emitted block used to fail ZERO of these cases. It is the key that
makes a translator see the block as inline base64 media at all: TypeScript
emits `source_type: "base64"` (`@langchain/core`'s `isDataContentBlock` tests
for `source_type` and nothing else) and Python emits the `base64` key itself
(measured on langchain-core 1.2.13: `is_data_content_block` returns True on
`"base64" in block`). A block that loses its marker is forwarded to the
provider as an unrecognized object — the exact failure the outbound design
exists to prevent. On the Python side the marker and the payload are the same
key, so `sourceType` there restates `data`; on the TypeScript side they are two
keys and this is the only thing pinning the marker.
An empty-string mimeType/filename is normalized to null on both sides: neither
runtime distinguishes "absent" from "present and empty" for those two fields,
and pinning a distinction the code does not make would be a false assertion.
WHAT THE PROJECTION DOES NOT COVER, stated so nobody has to rediscover it:
* Every key either runtime emits on an OUTBOUND block is projected. Nothing is
dropped there any more.
* INBOUND, only the AG-UI item's kind, source type, source value, MIME type and
`metadata.filename` are compared. Any OTHER key a runtime attached to
`metadata`, and the difference between an absent `metadata` and an empty one,
are invisible here.
* `""` and absent are the same value for `mimeType` and `filename` (above).
* Log PROSE is not compared, only the count — see the next section.
OUTBOUND INPUTS ARE DICTS. TypeScript's converter reads client JSON that nothing
validates. Python's reads pydantic-validated AG-UI content objects, so the suite
builds each item into its declared class; where a MALFORMED item cannot pass
validation, Python receives the raw dict, which is what its converter would see
for such an item in production (an item that fails validation is never a typed
content object). The two runtimes therefore reach some outbound drops through
DIFFERENT branches — TypeScript through a typed guard, Python through its
terminal `else`.
That divergence is expected, but it was left IMPLICIT and it made most of the
outbound malformed cases misdescribe themselves: eleven of twelve failed pydantic
validation and collapsed onto the single terminal `else`, so a case named after
a text guard or a media guard was not exercising one in Python at all. Two things
fix that:
* `outbound/malformed/ts-only/…` — the id says so. The named BRANCH is reached
in TypeScript only; in Python the item cannot become a typed content object,
so it arrives as a raw dict and lands in the terminal `else`. Both runtimes
still drop it and log once, which is what `expect` asserts.
* `pythonBuilds` — every outbound case records, per item, what Python's harness
actually builds it into (a class name, or `dict` / `NoneType` for an item no
class accepts). It is ASSERTED, so if a schema change ever moves a case onto a
different branch, the table says so instead of hiding it behind an unchanged
outcome triple.
KNOWN UNREACHABLE IN PYTHON: the legacy-binary `no url, data, or id` guard.
`BinaryInputContent` refuses to validate without one of the three, so no validated
item can reach that guard — only TypeScript's copy of it is live. That is why
`outbound/malformed/ts-only/binary-empty` carries the marker rather than being
reconstructed: there is no input that would reach the Python branch.
LOG PROSE IS NOT ASSERTED. `loggedDrops` counts warnings beginning "Dropping "
after prefix normalization. The rest of each message legitimately differs (`int`
vs `number`, `dict` vs `object`) and pinning it here would fail on wording.
`axis` is documentation only. `malformed` = input no schema allows; `edge` =
legal but easy to get wrong; `wellformed` = the modality x source x vocabulary
matrix that must not regress.
